text: Hiram Rhodes Revels (September 27, 1827 – January 16, 1901) was an American Republican politician, minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and college administrator. Born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, in 1827 to free people of color, Revels had ancestors who were free before the American Revolution; his parents were of African American, European, and Native American ancestry, with his mother specifically of Scots descent and his father a Baptist preacher. He received his early education from a local free Black woman despite restrictions on free Black children’s education and lived with his older brother Elias B. Revels in Lincolnton, North Carolina, where he was apprenticed as a barber in his brother’s shop—a trade considered respectable and socially beneficial for Black Americans at the time. After Elias Revels died in 1841, his widow transferred the shop to Hiram Revels. He attended the Beech Grove Quaker Seminary in Indiana and the Union Literary Institute (Darke County Seminary) in Randolph County, Indiana. In 1845, Revels was ordained as a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and served as a preacher and religious teacher in Indiana, Illinois, Ohio, Tennessee, Missouri, and Kansas; he was imprisoned in Missouri in 1854 for preaching to Black people but was never physically harmed. In the 1850s, he married Phoebe Bass, a free Black woman, and studied religion at Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois, before becoming a minister in Baltimore, Maryland, where he also served as principal of a Black high school. During the American Civil War, Revels served as a chaplain in the United States Army and helped organize two regiments of the United States Colored Troops in Maryland and Missouri, participating in the Battle of Vicksburg. In 1865, he left the AME Church to join the Methodist Episcopal Church and was assigned to churches in Leavenworth, Kansas, and New Orleans, Louisiana; in 1866, he became a permanent pastor in Natchez, Mississippi, where he settled with his wife and five daughters and became an elder in the Mississippi District of the Methodist Church. He founded schools for Black children during this time. In 1868, he was elected alderman in Natchez, and in 1869, he was elected to represent Adams County in the Mississippi State Senate. Congressman John R. Lynch noted that Revels was a new figure in the community, having never voted or attended political meetings, but was seen as intelligent and capable, and believed to be a man of ability. On January 1870, Revels delivered an impressive opening prayer in the Mississippi state legislature, which made a profound impression and led to his election to the U.S. Senate. In 1870, he was elected by a vote of 81 to 15 in the Mississippi legislature to fill the vacant U.S. Senate seat previously held by Albert G. Brown, who withdrew in 1861 when Mississippi seceded. When he arrived in Washington, D.C., Southern Democrats opposed his seating, citing the 1857 Dred Scott Decision, which held that Black people were not citizens, and arguing that Revels had not met the nine-year citizenship requirement before the 14th Amendment in 1868. Supporters countered that Revels had been a citizen since voting in Ohio and that the Civil War and Reconstruction amendments had overturned Dred Scott, making it unconstitutional to bar him based on pre-war constitutional rules. Senator Charles Sumner declared that "the time has passed for argument" and stated that colored persons must be senators, asserting that the Declaration of Independence’s principle of equality was now a reality. On February 25, 1870, Revels was seated in the U.S. Senate by a party-line vote of 48 to 8, with Republicans voting in favor and Democrats voting against, and everyone in the galleries stood to see him sworn in. Senator Henry Wilson defended Revels, citing signatures from Mississippi legislative clerks and Adelbert Ames, the military governor of Mississippi, and argued that skin color was not a barrier to Senate service, invoking the Golden Rule. Revels advocated compromise and moderation, supporting racial equality and urging fellow senators to recognize the capabilities of African Americans. In his maiden speech on March 16, 1870, he called for the reinstatement of Black legislators from Georgia who had been illegally removed. He served on the Committee of Education and Labor and the Committee on the District of Columbia, focusing on Reconstruction issues, and supported amnesty and full citizenship for former Confederates who swore loyalty to the United States. He opposed a proposal by Senator Allen G. Thurman to keep Washington, D.C. schools segregated and advocated for integration, nominated a young Black man to the U.S. Military Academy (who was denied admission), and successfully supported efforts to allow Black workers access to the Washington Navy Yard. The Northern press praised his oratory, and Congressman James G. Blaine noted that Black senators were studious, earnest, and honorable. Revels supported legislation to develop infrastructure in Mississippi, including grants for the New Orleans and Northeastern Railroad (41st Congress 2nd Session S. 712) and levees on the Mississippi River (41st Congress 3rd Session S. 1136). After his Senate term ended on March 3, 1871, Revels was appointed as the first president of Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College (now Alcorn State University) in Claiborne County, Mississippi, where he taught philosophy. In 1873, he took a leave of absence to serve as Mississippi’s secretary of state ad interim. He was dismissed from Alcorn in 1874 after campaigning against the reelection of Governor Adelbert Ames and was reappointed in 1876 by the new Democratic administration, serving until his retirement in 1882. On November 6, 1875, Revels wrote a letter to President Ulysses S. Grant denouncing Adelbert Ames and carpetbaggers for manipulating the Black vote and perpetuating racial hatred. He remained active as a Methodist Episcopal minister in Holly Springs, Mississippi, becoming an elder in the Upper Mississippi District and serving briefly as editor of the Southwestern Christian Advocate. He also taught theology at Shaw College (now Rust College). Hiram Revels died on January 16, 1901, while attending a church conference in Aberdeen, Mississippi, and was buried at Hillcrest Cemetery in Holly Springs. His daughter, Susie Revels Cayton, edited The Seattle Republican in Seattle, Washington, and among his grandsons were Horace R. Cayton Jr., co-author of Black Metropolis, and Revels Cayton, a labor leader. In 2002, scholar Molefi Kete Asante listed Hiram Rhodes Revels as one of the 100 Greatest African Americans.
